Woman of Valor
wụm´an ŭv văl´ẽr
n. phrase (the wife of Proverbs 31; Hebrew eshet chayil, a woman of strength or force)
Hebrew chayil is strength, army, wealth, might — the word used of a soldier's valour and a nation's forces. The Authorized Version renders eshet chayil as a virtuous woman, which is true and softer than the Hebrew.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

“Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies” (Pro 31:10). The poem that follows is an acrostic describing a woman who buys a field, plants a vineyard, trades profitably, works in wool and flax, gives to the poor, is clothed with strength and honour, and opens her mouth with wisdom. Its verdict is not on any of that: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Pro 31:30). Boaz uses the same phrase of Ruth: “all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman” (Rut 3:11), and Proverbs elsewhere: “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband” (Pro 12:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines virtuous as morally good; acting in conformity to the moral law; and, applied to women, chaste; and valor as strength of mind in regard to danger, courage, prowess.

expand to see more

VIRTUOUS, a. Morally good; acting in conformity to the moral law; practicing the moral duties, and abstaining from vice.

2. Being in conformity to the moral or divine law.

3. Chaste; applied to women.

VALOR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; that quality which enables a man to encounter danger with firmness; personal bravery; courage; prowess.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:10 — "Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies."

Pro 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

Rut 3:11 — "And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman."

Pro 12:4 — "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones."

Pro 31:25 — "Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come."

Modern Corruption

Proverbs 31 is used to exhaust women with a checklist, and the poem is an alphabet of praise ending in the fear of the LORD.

expand to see more

The chapter is regularly preached as a specification, with the result that Christian women read the Bible's most extravagant compliment as a performance review. Two features of the text resist that. It is an acrostic — twenty-two verses running the Hebrew alphabet, a form used for praise and completeness rather than for instruction — and it is placed in the mouth of a mother teaching a king what to look for in a wife, not in the mouth of a husband telling a wife what to be. It is a portrait, and portraits are not schedules.

The Hebrew of the title is stronger than any English rendering. Chayil is the word for an army, for wealth, for might; it is used of mighty men of valour, and the same phrase applied to a man would be translated a mighty warrior. The AV's virtuous is accurate to the moral sense and loses the muscle. The woman of this poem buys real estate, runs a business, arms herself with strength, and laughs at the time to come; a reading that reduces her to domestic gentleness has translated the word down.

And the poem judges itself in verse 30. After twenty verses of competence — the merchandise, the candle burning at night, the tapestry, the fine linen sold to the merchant — the summary sets all of it aside: favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. Every accomplishment listed can be counterfeited by a woman without the fear of God, and none of it is the ground of the praise. That is the same verdict the whole book of Proverbs gives on everything else, and it arrives, deliberately, on the last page.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew eshet chayil (H802, H2428), a woman of strength, force, valour; yare (H3372), to fear; oz (H5797), strength.

expand to see more

Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, army, wealth, valour; Proverbs 31:10, 12:4, Ruth 3:11; and of soldiers, Judges 6:12, 1 Samuel 16:18.

Hebrew oz (H5797) — strength; Proverbs 31:17, 31:25, “strength and honour are her clothing.”

Hebrew yirat YHWH (H3374) — the fear of the LORD; Proverbs 31:30, 1:7, 9:10.

Usage

"“Who can find a virtuous woman?” — the Hebrew word would be valour in a man."

"“Strength and honour are her clothing” — the muscle the English softens."

"“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain” — the poem setting its own list aside."
